deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated parts.

(A) Lines 1-17 are a personal note on priority, continuing a sentence from the previous page. Hilbert has heard, via Minkowski from Hensel and via Eberhard from Gutzmer, that people in Berlin say his work contains nothing that is not already in Kronecker's investigations. He has also heard that his invariant-theoretic papers are 'only a transfer of Kronecker's ideas into invariant theory'; Kronecker himself reportedly said this with Gutzmer present.

Hilbert rejects this.
- Even the concept of a module (Modul), which he says does not really originate with Kronecker anyway, is essentially modified in his work by the requirement of homogeneity. In modern terms, he works with homogeneous ideals in k[x_1,...,x_n].
- All further concepts, methods and results are his own. He names in particular the 'erste Fundamentalsatz', i.e. the finite basis theorem (Hilbert Basis Theorem, 1888/1890).
- He expects any decent person to help correct this 'obvious error'.
There is no mathematical derivation here.

(B) Lines 18-21 begin a research note that continues on the next page. Let f be a form of order n. If f is to be written as a sum of n-th powers of linear forms, f = sum_{i=1}^{s} l_i^n, one must ask how many-valued ('vieldeutig') this representation is.

His proposed method (completed on the next page):
1. Study the 'discriminant locus': the condition under which two of the representations coincide.
2. Follow how the different representations pass into one another when one circles this locus.

In modern terms: consider the finite map from s-tuples of linear forms to forms, (l_1,...,l_s) -> sum l_i^n, in the case where the parameter count matches, s*k = binom(n+k-1, k-1) for k variables. One studies the branch locus of this map. The monodromy (Galois) group acting on the generic fibre then describes how the decompositions are permuted.

The classic cases of this kind are:
- binary forms of degree 2s-1, with a unique decomposition (Sylvester);
- quaternary cubics as sums of 5 cubes (Sylvester's pentahedral theorem);
- ternary quintics as sums of 7 fifth powers, which Hilbert himself asserted (1888) to be unique.

No computation is carried out on this page; it states a programme only.
errors: None mathematical. Small point: for the cases best known from the literature (Sylvester's binary forms, the pentahedral theorem, ternary quintics) the generic decomposition is unique, so the monodromy question is trivial there. The programme is only non-trivial when the generic number of decompositions is greater than 1, e.g. in cases with a positive-dimensional family or several decompositions; Hilbert does not say which cases he has in mind.

results.what: Claim that his module concept (homogeneous modules/ideals) and his first fundamental theorem (finite basis theorem) are original and not a transfer of Kronecker's ideas
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (1888/1890); module concept from Dedekind, Kronecker's Modulsysteme

results.what: Question of how many-valued the Waring decomposition of a form is, to be studied via the branch (discriminant) locus and the monodromy of the decompositions around it
results.modern_name: Identifiability of Waring (symmetric tensor) decompositions; monodromy/Galois group of decompositions
results.usually_credited_to: Uniqueness cases: Sylvester (1851), Hilbert (1888, ternary quintics), Palatini/Richmond (~1903-04). Monodromy approach: modern numerical algebraic geometry, e.g. Hauenstein-Oeding-Ottaviani-Sommese (2016)

deep.surprise_reason: The priority remarks about Kronecker are of biographical interest, but Hilbert's tensions with the Berlin school are well documented. The Waring note is only a programmatic idea, though an early monodromy-style view of decomposition multiplicity. It fits Hilbert's known 1888 interest in sums of powers (the ternary quintic claim), so it is only mildly notable.

checkable.asserts: Parameter count for ternary quintics: 21 coefficients equal 7 linear forms times 3 coefficients, so a sum of 7 fifth powers is expected to be finite-to-one (Hilbert's uniqueness case).
Quaternary cubics: 20 coefficients equal 5 linear forms times 4, the Sylvester pentahedral case.
Binary forms of degree 2s-1 have 2s coefficients, matching s binary linear forms (Sylvester's uniqueness case).
Ternary quartics: the naive count suggests 5 fourth powers, but this case is defective (Clebsch); 6 are needed.
